title: How do you implement RSocket error handling, and what happens on client/server disconnect (onErrorResume, retryWhen, keep-alive, resumption)?
shortTitle: How do you implement RSocket error handling, and what happens on client/server disconnect (onErrorResume, retryWhen, keep-alive, resumption)?

s1_definition.profdef: RSocket error handling operates at two layers. At the stream layer, errors are delivered as Reactive Streams error signals on the `Mono`/`Flux`, so you handle them with Reactor operators like `onErrorResume` (substitute a fallback), `onErrorReturn` (substitute a value), and `retryWhen` (retry with a policy such as exponential backoff). At the connection layer, RSocket uses periodic keep-alive frames to detect dead peers, raises connection errors when liveness fails, and supports session resumption so a dropped TCP connection can be re-established and the logical streams continued using a resume token, without the application losing in-flight stream state. On disconnect without resumption, active streams terminate with an error and the client typically reconnects and retries.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh is on a live call with National Bank of India's trading desk. If the desk hits a problem answering one question, it tells Rajesh "that failed," and Rajesh's app can either show a cached fallback (onErrorResume) or politely ask again a moment later (retryWhen with backoff). Meanwhile the phone line itself has a heartbeat: both sides say "still there?" every few seconds (keep-alive). If the line drops, the system can dial back and pick up the exact same conversation where it left off using a claim ticket (resume token), so Rajesh does not lose his place in the live price feed.
s1_definition.oneliner: Handle per-stream errors with onErrorResume and retryWhen, detect dead peers with keep-alive, and survive drops with resumption tokens; without resumption, streams error out and the client reconnects.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** RSocket error handling operates at two layers. At the stream layer, errors are delivered as Reactive Streams error signals on the `Mono`/`Flux`, so you handle them with Reactor operators like `onErrorResume` (substitute a fallback), `onErrorReturn` (substitute a value), and `retryWhen` (retry with a policy such as exponential backoff). At the connection layer, RSocket uses periodic keep-alive frames to detect dead peers, raises connection errors when liveness fails, and supports session resumption so a dropped TCP connection can be re-established and the logical streams continued using a resume token, without the application losing in-flight stream state. On disconnect without resumption, active streams terminate with an error and the client typically reconnects and retries.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh is on a live call with National Bank of India's trading desk. If the desk hits a problem answering one question, it tells Rajesh "that failed," and Rajesh's app can either show a cached fallback (onErrorResume) or politely ask again a moment later (retryWhen with backoff). Meanwhile the phone line itself has a heartbeat: both sides say "still there?" every few seconds (keep-alive). If the line drops, the system can dial back and pick up the exact same conversation where it left off using a claim ticket (resume token), so Rajesh does not lose his place in the live price feed.

**One line to remember:** Handle per-stream errors with onErrorResume and retryWhen, detect dead peers with keep-alive, and survive drops with resumption tokens; without resumption, streams error out and the client reconnects.

sections.s2_technical:
Stream-level errors arrive as Reactor error signals. On the client you compose recovery operators directly on the returned publisher. For example `requester.route("account.balance").data(id).retrieveMono(BalanceResponse.class).onErrorResume(ex -> Mono.just(cachedBalance(id)))` returns a cached balance if the server call fails. `retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofSeconds(1)))` retries up to three times with exponential backoff and jitter, which is the right default for transient faults. On the server, you throw or return an errored `Mono`/`Flux`, and Spring maps exceptions; you can centralize mapping with an `@MessageExceptionHandler` method that converts a domain exception into a clean error payload so the client sees a structured error rather than a raw stack trace.

Keep-alive is the connection liveness mechanism. Both peers exchange KEEPALIVE frames at a configured interval, and if no acknowledgment arrives within the max-lifetime window, the connection is considered dead and torn down, surfacing as a connection error to any active streams. You tune these with the client setup: for example a keep-alive interval of 20 seconds and a max lifetime of 90 seconds balances fast dead-peer detection against tolerance for brief network hiccups.

Resumption is what distinguishes a graceful recovery from a hard failure. When you enable resume on the connection, RSocket negotiates a resume token; if the transport drops, the client reconnects and presents the token, and the protocol replays unacknowledged frames so the logical streams continue, meaning a long-running price stream survives a transient network blip without the subscriber seeing an error. If resumption is not enabled, a disconnect terminates active streams with an error signal, and the standard pattern is for the client to reconnect and re-subscribe, often guided by `retryWhen` on the connection or stream. Senior nuances: make requests idempotent so retries are safe, especially for anything that moves money; set retry limits and backoff with jitter to avoid retry storms; distinguish retryable errors (timeouts, connection resets) from non-retryable ones (validation errors) and only retry the former with a predicate like `Retry.backoff(3, ...).filter(this::isTransient)`; and for request-channel sessions decide whether to resume the channel or restart it from a known checkpoint. In a banking context I also ensure fire-and-forget is never used for money movement, because its delivery is not guaranteed, and I reserve it for best-effort telemetry.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Rajesh's trading app queries his balance over RSocket, but the backend occasionally has a transient glitch. The app must not show an error for a momentary blip. This is exactly what onErrorResume and retryWhen solve — retry transient failures, and fall back to a cached balance if all retries fail.

Problem 2 — Rajesh subscribes to a live price feed, and his mobile network briefly drops. Losing the feed and all its state would be a poor experience. This is exactly what keep-alive plus session resumption solve — the dropped connection reconnects with a resume token and the feed continues.

The demo configures an RSocket client with keep-alive and resume, queries a balance with retry and fallback, and subscribes to a price stream that survives a simulated disconnect. Classes and steps: `ResilientTradingClient` (configures keep-alive + resume, applies retry/fallback), `BalanceResponse`/`PriceTick` (DTOs), and a Spring `@MessageExceptionHandler` on the controller for server-side mapping.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh queries balance for SAV2001; then subscribes to the RELIANCE price feed; a transient network drop occurs mid-feed.

Step 1 — The client connects with keep-alive every 20 seconds and resume enabled, so a resume token is negotiated at setup.

Step 2 — The balance query is sent. Suppose the first attempt fails with a transient connection error. `retryWhen` matches the transient predicate and retries with exponential backoff, logging each attempt. On a successful retry it returns Rajesh's Rs.1,000,000.

Step 3 — If all three retries fail, `onErrorResume` fires and the client returns the cached balance instead of surfacing an error, so Rajesh still sees a number with a "may be stale" indication.

Step 4 — On the price feed, a transient drop occurs. Because resume is enabled, RSocket reconnects using the resume token and replays unacknowledged frames, so the subscriber continues receiving ticks without seeing an error. If resumption had been off, the stream would error, and the `retryWhen` on the flux would reconnect and re-subscribe instead.

```
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [WARN] Retrying balance for SAV2001 attempt 1
2026-10-26 14:55:12 [INFO] Balance resolved: SAV2001 Rs.1000000
2026-10-26 14:55:12 [INFO] Tick 0 Rs.2450
2026-10-26 14:55:14 [WARN] connection dropped — resuming session with token
2026-10-26 14:55:14 [INFO] Tick 1 Rs.2451
```

```text

    │
    ├─ balance "SAV2001"
    │    │ attempt 1 FAIL (transient)
    │    │ retryWhen backoff → attempt 2 OK → Rs.1,000,000
    │    └─ all retries fail → onErrorResume → cached Rs.1,000,000

    └─ price.stream "RELIANCE"  (limitRate 3)

```

```
  ═══ LLD — RSocket Error Handling ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Retry + Backoff: Retry.backoff with transient filter           │
  │    WHY: recover transient faults without retry storms          │
  │ Fallback/Circuit-ish: onErrorResume → cached value             │
  │    WHY: degrade gracefully instead of erroring the user        │

  │    WHY: survive transport drops without losing stream state    │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: client handles resilience; controller handles mapping       │
  │ O: new error type = new predicate / handler, no rewrites       │
  │ D: client depends on RSocketRequester + Reactor abstractions   │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Stream Lifecycle ───────────────────────────
  [CONNECTED] ──drop──→ [RESUMING] ──token ok──→ [CONNECTED]
       │                    │
       │ no resume / fail   ▼
       │               [ERROR] ──retryWhen──→ [RECONNECTING] → [CONNECTED]
       ▼
  [COMPLETED]

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. balanceWithResilience(id) → retrieveMono
  2.   → retryWhen(backoff, filter=transient)
  3.   → onErrorResume → cachedBalance
  4. subscribePrices(symbol) → resume on drop OR retryWhen reconnect
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
RSocket error handling works at two layers, and I always talk about both. At the stream layer, errors arrive as Reactive Streams error signals, so I handle them with Reactor operators. I use retryWhen with exponential backoff and jitter to recover transient faults, and I filter it with a predicate so I only retry retryable errors like timeouts and connection resets, never validation errors. When all retries are exhausted, I use onErrorResume or onErrorReturn to degrade gracefully, for example returning a cached balance instead of showing Rajesh an error. On the server I centralize mapping with a message exception handler so the client receives a clean, structured error rather than a raw stack trace.

At the connection layer, RSocket uses keep-alive frames to detect dead peers. Both sides ping at a configured interval, and if acknowledgments stop arriving within the max-lifetime window, the connection is declared dead and active streams receive a connection error. I tune the keep-alive interval and lifetime to balance fast detection against tolerance for brief hiccups.

The most important part on disconnect is resumption. When I enable resume, the connection negotiates a resume token, and if the transport drops, the client reconnects, presents the token, and the protocol replays unacknowledged frames so the logical streams continue. In my banking work at National Bank of India this means Rajesh's live price feed survives a brief mobile-network blip without his subscriber ever seeing an error. If resumption is not enabled, a disconnect terminates the active streams with an error, and the client simply reconnects and re-subscribes, which I drive with retryWhen on the stream or connection.

The senior points I always add are that retries must be safe, so I make requests idempotent, especially anything touching money, I cap retries and add jitter to avoid retry storms, and I never use fire-and-forget for money movement because its delivery is not guaranteed. So my summary answer is: handle per-stream errors with retryWhen and onErrorResume, detect dead peers with keep-alive, and survive drops with session resumption, and where resumption is not possible, reconnect and retry idempotently.
